item.title: Takaichi calls China 'important neighbor' but hypes 'regional' tensions; experts say rhetoric masks continued provocation
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-05 23:44:00
Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi delivers a policy speech at a plenary session of the House of Representatives on October 5, 2026. Photo: VCG Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi on Monday called China an "important neighbor" and said Japan would advance its strategic relationship of mutual benefit, with China, while claiming that it would firmly "assert" its positions on issues including the East and South China Seas and what it called China's "regional military activities," and demanding that China take "responsible actions," Kyodo News reported. Some Chinese experts said Takaichi's remarks were a perfunctory response to mounting pressure both at home and abroad, with the conciliatory rhetoric aimed at placating Japan's business community amid closely intertwined China-Japan supply chains and calls for the restoration of normal economic and trade ties. However, the Japanese government's fundamental stance toward China has not changed, and the remarks essentially amount to another provocation against China. Takaichi made those remarks during a policy speech on Monday in both Diet chambers, according to Japanese media reports. Referring to China as an "important neighbor" despite increasingly strained bilateral ties, she said Japan would strengthen communication on "common challenges" and promote dialogue aimed at protecting Japan's national interests, the Sankei Shimbun reported. Takaichi also seized on what she framed as heightened, assertive Chinese military posturing in the East China Sea and South China Sea, some Japanese media reports said. She claimed Japan would "vigorously press its own claims" and press China to behave in what Japan deems a responsible manner. Meanwhile, she noted that the two countries have longstanding ties despite of the existence of certain issues, and said Japan would continue to advance its strategic relationship of mutual benefit, according to Japanese media reports. Lü Chao, an expert at the Liaoning Academy of Social Sciences, told the Global Times on Monday that Takaichi's remarks were aimed at responding to mounting pressure from Japan's business community. With China and Japan closely intertwined through their supply and industrial chains, political confrontation due to Takaichi's erroneous remarks about China's Taiwan island has seriously affected economic and trade cooperation. As a Japanese economic delegation recently visited China and calls grow from various quarters to restore normal economic and trade exchanges, Takaichi is attempting to ease domestic pressure by making verbal gestures of easing tensions and providing an explanation to Japan's business community, Lü said. Meanwhile, China has continued to strongly criticize Takaichi's erroneous positions in international forums, with 33rd Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) Economic Leaders' Meeting to be held in Shenzhen, South China's Guangdong Province, in November also approaching. Takaichi's perfunctory remarks were a response to pressure both at home and abroad, aimed at using the occasion to project a certain stance, while her fundamental position remains unchanged, the expert said. During the policy address, Takaichi also claimed Japan would strengthen its defense capabilities and intelligence functions, claiming that the security environment surrounding Japan was changing at an "astonishing speed" and becoming increasingly complex and severe. She said Japan would revise its three key security documents by the end of the year in order to "fundamentally strengthen defense capabilities," the Asahi Shimbun reported. "The Japanese government was deliberately portraying the regional security situation as increasingly dangerous and creating a tense atmosphere to prepare public opinion for moves to break through the principle of 'exclusively defense-oriented policy' and three principles on transfer of defense equipment and technology," the expert noted. Lü further criticized the Takaichi administration for displaying a more extreme right-wing tendency than previous Japanese administrations. Its main dangerous moves include continuously increasing defense spending and developing offensive weapons and weapons of mass destruction, easing restrictions on arms exports to promote Japanese military products overseas, and challenging international norms by advocating the removal of the "enemy state clauses" in the UN Charter, Lü said. China's top diplomat Wang Yi met with Takeshi Iwaya, president of the Japanese Association for the Promotion of International Trade (JAPIT), in Beijing on September 28, the Xinhua News Agency reported. Noting that this year marks the 80th anniversary of the opening of the Tokyo Trials, Wang, director of the Office of the Foreign Affairs Commission of the Communist Party of China Central Committee and a member of the Political Bureau of the Communist Party of China Central Committee, said that Japan is once again facing the test of history, Xinhua noted. If Japan refuses to learn from historical lessons, challenges the post-war pacifist Constitution, denies its history of aggression or glorifies war criminals, it cannot face the world and there's no building a future to speak of, Wang said, per Xinhua. Noting that next year marks the 55th anniversary of the normalization of diplomatic relations between China and Japan, Wang said what matters is to adopt a correct attitude on historical issues. Fundamentally, Japan needs to develop an objective and rational perception of China, he added, Xinhua said.

item.title: Ancient temple draws visitors as cultural tourism booms in Shanxi
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-05 20:43:00
For years, Yang Liangen saw strangers as a threat. After a series of break-in attempts at a 900-year-old temple in north China's Shanxi Province, Yang moved into the compound in 1997, sleeping behind its gates and guarding its rare sculptures and wooden structures. Nearly three decades later, he eagerly waits for strangers to arrive. "We used to be afraid when people came," Yang said. "Now we hope they will come." Located in Xiaonan Village in Jincheng City, Erxian Temple fully opened to the public in 2024 as interest in Shanxi's ancient architecture surged following the release of "Black Myth: Wukong," a blockbuster Chinese video game. During China's National Day holiday that year, Yang counted 1,280 visitors in a single day -- a record for a site whose gates had long been kept mostly shut. The crowds have continued to grow, with more than 4,300 people visiting the temple from Oct. 1 to 3 this year. The change at Erxian Temple reflects a broader shift across China, as growing interest in cultural tourism brings new attention to historic buildings that for decades were little known beyond their local communities. Tourists visit Foguang Temple in Xinzhou City of north China's Shanxi Province, July 15, 2026. (Xinhua/Xu Xiaoxuan) Built in 1097, Erxian Temple is a major national cultural heritage site. Its main hall is known for rare Song Dynasty (960-1279) painted sculptures and an exceptionally well-preserved miniature wooden architectural structure known locally as the "sky bridge." Dubbed China's "above-ground cultural relics museum," Shanxi is home to over 28,000 ancient structures. The province also preserves more than 12,000 painted sculptures and 24,000 square meters of murals from the Tang Dynasty (618-907) onward. PRESERVED BEHIND THE GATES For Yang, the new attention marks a dramatic change from the late 1990s. Facing growing risks to the temple in 1997, Yang, then the village Party secretary, took responsibility for Erxian Temple and moved in with his wife. The couple kept watch day and night. On one occasion, Yang's wife rushed outside with a flashlight after two people were spotted apparently chiseling through a wall, sending them fleeing. No theft has occurred since Yang became its caretaker. A major restoration completed in 2014 repaired the compound and revived its two-courtyard layout. Surveillance cameras were installed, giving the couple what Yang described as their first truly restful sleep in years. But the gates largely remained closed. Visits by preservation experts became important opportunities for Yang. He followed them around, learning about Song Dynasty construction and the temple's rare architectural features. As architecture enthusiasts began making their way to the village, Yang sometimes made exceptions to let them inside and shared what he had learned. "They had come such a long way," Yang said. "Maybe they would only come once in their lives. How could I not let them see it?" Over time, Yang turned himself from a guard into an unofficial guide. FINDING NEW AUDIENCES Years of restoration and improved security eventually made it possible for more people to see what Yang had spent decades protecting. In late 2022, an upgrade of Erxian Temple's security system was launched. Around the same time, local heritage enthusiasts formed a volunteer association in Jincheng City to support heritage site caretakers, organize educational visits and train volunteer guides. In August 2024, Jincheng began opening 18 nationally and provincially protected heritage sites to the public on Sundays on a trial basis before fully opening them in October. Erxian Temple was included. "The temple didn't become popular overnight," said Zhang Jianjun, one of the association's founders. "Without all those years of preparation, we wouldn't have been ready when the crowds came." The association now has more than 400 members, including Zhang Jie, a local charter driver who first visited Erxian Temple while taking customers around Shanxi in 2024. Standing among centuries-old sculptures and elaborate woodwork, he realized how little he knew about the heritage of his own home province. "I felt ashamed, but also curious," he said. He began studying traditional architecture, joined the volunteer association and now shares what he has learned with tourists. At the Hanging Temple in Datong City, Chen Ruiyan recalled a recent road trip she and her husband had taken from Guangdong Province to Shanxi, visiting more than a dozen historic sites across the province. Inspired by films and animations featuring Shanxi's ancient architecture, they had studied traditional architectural features before setting out. "Beyond their aesthetic impact, ancient wooden buildings have a sense of quietness and vitality," Chen said. This photo taken on Feb. 28, 2025 shows the Hanging Temple, or Xuankong Temple, in Hunyuan County, Datong City in north China's Shanxi Province. (Xinhua/Yang Chenguang) Beyond Shanxi, efforts to preserve historic architecture are also bringing old buildings closer to contemporary life. In Fujian Province, traditional Tulou, or earthen buildings, are being preserved and given new uses, while in Guizhou Province, more than 12,000 endangered traditional buildings have undergone emergency restoration. China's latest five-year plan for cultural heritage calls for stronger systematic protection while making preservation efforts more accessible and beneficial to the public. Wang Chunbo, a researcher specializing in ancient architecture, sculptures and murals in Shanxi, said the growing interest in historic architecture reflects a deeper engagement with traditional culture among younger Chinese. "Young people are no longer satisfied with simply checking a destination off their list," Wang said. "Historic buildings are becoming cultural spaces they can experience, engage with and share." Li Junda, a university student studying anthropology in London, traveled to Shanxi after encountering Yang's story online. What struck him was how the temple's history was still carried by the people around it. "At the British Museum, I saw many Chinese artifacts on display, identified simply by their dynasties," Li said. "Here in Shanxi, the heritage is still 'alive,' because villagers like Yang are here to tell the stories behind it."

item.title: China's largest desert oilfield extracts over 26 million tons of oil and gas from depths below 6,000 meters
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-05 20:42:00
A view of the Fuman Oilfield, located on the northern edge of the Taklimakan Desert in Northwest China's Xinjiang Uygur Autonomous Region. File photo: China Media Group China's largest desert oilfield, the Fuman Oilfield located on the northern edge of the Taklimakan Desert in Northwest China's Xinjiang Uygur Autonomous Region, has extracted over 26 million tons of oil and gas from depths below 6,000 meters, hitting a major milestone, China National Petroleum Corp (CNPC), the operator of the oilfield, said on Monday. Recently, at the Zhentan-1 well on the edge of the Taklimakan Desert, engineers pulled up rock cores from 8,080 meters underground - rocks that have been buried for about 500 million years. This marks the first time that China has retrieved a core sample from a depth of more than 8,000 meters in the northwestern Tarim Basin. The Taklimakan Desert lies in the heart of the Tarim Basin in southern Xinjiang, and forms the main body of this vast inland basin. "With these precious rock cores, we can analyze and evaluate the hydrocarbon generation potential below 8,000 meters, including the thickness of the oil and gas layers and their maturity levels," Xu Yanan, director of Tarim Oilfield project at CNPC, was quoted as saying in a report by the China Central Television (CCTV) News. "We have already extracted 20.36 million tons of crude oil and 8.15 billion cubic meters of natural gas from the ultra-deep formations beneath the Taklimakan Desert, with a combined oil and gas equivalent exceeding 26.86 million tons," said Lu Zhongyuan, an engineer at CNPC's Tarim Oilfield, per the CCTV report. In recent years, the Tarim Oilfield has stepped up ultra-deep oil and gas production in the Taklimakan Desert. At the Fuman Oilfield, a total of 485 ultra-deep wells have been drilled. Among them, 133 wells have each produced more than 100,000 tons of oil and gas in total, and 464 wells have each produced more than 10,000 tons. This has made the Tarim Oilfield China's largest desert oilfield and ultra-deep hydrocarbon production base, according to media reports. The ultra-deep formations in the Tarim Basin hold abundant oil and gas reserves and represent an important potential area for increasing China's hydrocarbon reserves and production. China has already proven more than 5 billion tons of oil and gas reserves in the Tarim Basin, with over half of them coming from ultra-deep layers, or more than 6,000 meters underground. item.title: Tokyo expresses 'regret,' lodges protest over a US Marine killing in Okinawa. Then what?
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-05 19:35:00
People hold a march calling for the burden on Okinawa from hosting US forces to be lifted in Okinawa on May 14, 2022. Photo: VCG A US service member causes a tragedy on Japanese soil. Japan expresses "regret," lodges a "strong protest," and demands measures to "prevent a recurrence." The US says it will fully cooperate with the investigation. The language is strong. The tone is grave. And then what? The bases remain. Military aircraft keep taking off and landing. The military buildup continues. When the next case comes, Tokyo will go through much the same script. This time, the victim is 39-year-old Anna Yagi, who died in a hotel in Naha, Okinawa. Next time, who will it be? A US Marine was arrested Sunday on suspicion of murder and robbery after Yagi's body was discovered in a hotel room in Okinawa. Reports cited police as saying that Yagi had "died from suffocation after being strangled." The case prompted outrage across Japan, and the Japanese government was compelled to put on a show of anger. The Japanese government quickly started an almost predictable crisis-response routine: Foreign Minister Toshimitsu Motegi summoned the US ambassador; Defense Minister Shinjiro Koizumi lodged a protest with the commander of US Forces Japan; and Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi expressed regret on social media and demanded that the US military tighten discipline on October 4. A day later, before her policy speech in the House of Representatives, she said it again: the crime was "extremely regrettable." Japan had lodged a strong protest, she added, and demanded full cooperation, stricter discipline, and measures to prevent a recurrence. The question is: What actually changes when Japan repeats the same words again and again? Take a look at the numbers. According to police figures cited in reports, Okinawa police cleared 6,235 criminal cases involving US service members, base employees, and their relatives from 1972 to 2023. Of these, 586 were serious offenses, including murder, robbery, and sexual assault. In 2024, a US serviceman was sentenced to five years for kidnapping and raping a Japanese schoolgirl. The Japanese side stressed the need to take measures to prevent a recurrence. Yet similar cases followed. A total of 101 criminal charges were filed against US military personnel and others connected to the US military in Okinawa Prefecture in 2025, according to prefectural police. It was the first time in 22 years - since 2003 - that the tentative figure had surpassed 100. The promise is always the same: tighten discipline, prevent a recurrence. Yet the crimes are not. What, then, do the promises mean? Perhaps the most disturbing thing is not whether any one protest was strong enough. It is how familiar the sequence has become. The same pattern repeats again and again. For Tokyo, the US-Japan alliance is a so-called national security imperative. For Washington, it is a regional strategy. For ordinary people in Okinawa, it is first of all the place where they live. For years, they have experienced the alliance as noise, accidents, crime, military bases, and the constant worry of not knowing what will happen next. On October 4, Okinawa's newly elected governor, Genta Koja, told reporters that the fact that this kind of event has happened again leaves us no choice but to conclude that the US military's efforts in maintaining discipline, educating personnel, and other such measures are completely ineffective. On October 5, Japanese media quoted former upper house member Keiko Itokazu as saying that Okinawans, especially women, should not have to keep bearing this grief and pain. She said that each time, the Japanese government and the US military have claimed to impose stricter discipline and provide proper education for service members. "Is this the result of the so-called education?" she asked, warning that if the bases expand and the number of US troops grows, the harm is likely to grow. In Western foreign-policy discourse, "ally" is a common word. It suggests equality, respect, and mutual support. But who is kept safe? Who carries the risk? Who decides where that risk falls? And who is allowed to say no? Those are the questions that word should bring into the open. That is also why a criminal case can eventually become a political mirror. In that mirror, there is certainly the individual responsibility of the US service member involved. But there is also Japan's own choice. Some observers have therefore argued that Japan's protests are largely for show. Okinawa is home to more than 40 US military bases, about 70 percent of all the US bases in Japan. In recent years, despite sustained local opposition, Tokyo has continued to expand both its own military presence and the US footprint there. Step by step, the prefecture is being turned into a forward bastion. The US-Japan Status of Forces Agreement was signed in 1960. Under Article 17, the US has primary jurisdiction when service members commit crimes in the performance of official duty. Whether an act is deemed to have been committed in the performance of official duty is largely determined by the US side. On August 20, 2026, the governors of 15 prefectures with US bases petitioned Tokyo for a fundamental revision of the agreement. But so far, public reporting has shown no commitment to revise it. Repeated crimes by US military personnel have been met with the same promises and little visible change. Many cases involving US military personnel in Japan have gone unresolved. That is part of the situation Okinawa lives with today. The contradiction is familiar. The number of crimes remains high. The bases have not moved. Protest has become a form of diplomatic theater. It raises a hard question: is Tokyo trying to solve Okinawa's problem, or only to manage Okinawa's anger about it? A woman is dead in a hotel in Naha. Her name was Anna Yagi. Her death is likely, sooner or later, to be overtaken by the next case involving US personnel and become another line in Okinawa's long record of such harm. The Japanese government will probably issue another statement of "strong protest." Sometimes, this is what being an ally looks like.

item.title: PLA Southern Theater Command expels Philippine aircraft from China's Huangyan Dao airspace in accordance with laws
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-05 17:53:00
PLA Southern Theater Command expels Philippine aircraft from China's Huangyan Dao airspace in accordance with laws By Shen Sheng Published: Oct 05, 2026 05:53 PM Updated: Oct 05, 2026 07:40 PM On October 3, a Philippine C-208 aircraft illegally intruded into the territorial airspace over China's Huangyan Dao without approval from the Chinese government. The naval and air forces dispatched by the PLA Southern Theater Command (STC) tracked and monitored the Philippine aircraft, and issued warnings to expel it in accordance with laws and regulations, Senior Captain Zhai Shichen, spokesperson for the PLA STC, said on Monday. Huangyan Dao is China's inherent territory. The acts by the Philippine side seriously violate China's sovereignty and are highly likely to cause unintended maritime and air incidents, the spokesperson said. We sternly warn the Philippine side to stop rights-violation and provocative acts immediately. Forces of the STC remain on high alert at all times to firmly safeguard national sovereignty and security as well as regional peace and stability, Zhai noted. A video footage released by the PLA STC showed a J-16 fighter jet carrying live PL-10 missile while carrying out the operation to drive away the aircraft. Song Zhongping, a Chinese military affairs expert, noted that carrying live ammunition is now a routine deployment measure for Chinese warplanes. If an opposing military aircraft continues to provoke China or takes provocative actions carrying irreversible risks that threaten China's sovereignty and the security of its territorial waters and airspace, Chinese warplanes can use all necessary means to safeguard China's sovereignty, Song said. "This means that we can use all available means, including equipping aircraft with live ammunition. When it comes to safeguarding national sovereignty and security, the J-16 leaves no room for ambiguity. Carrying live ammunition on missions is both a routine arrangement and a strong deterrent and stern warning to intruders," he said. The Philippine Star on Sunday claimed that the J-16 "maneuvered directly ahead of and around the C-208," creating what the Armed Forces of the Philippines (AFP) described as a "serious aviation safety risk." The airspace over areas including Huangyan Dao belongs to China and is inviolable, Song noted. China's interception of any aircraft or vessels that illegally intrude into the area is justified, reasonable and lawful, and complies with both domestic and international law, he said. "If the Philippines continues to escalate provocations and ultimately triggers an accident, the responsibility will rest entirely with the Philippine side, which will have to bear the consequences," Song said.

item.title: UN official highlights GDI's role in advancing sustainable development
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-05 16:42:00
Dima Al-Khatib (L, Front), director of the UN Office for South-South Cooperation, speaks at a high-level panel discussion on South-South cooperation, at the UN headquarters in New York, on Sept. 12, 2024. Photo: Xinhua Five years after China proposed the Global Development Initiative (GDI), its focus is shifting increasingly towards practical cooperation that addresses the priorities of developing countries, a senior UN official has said. "Five years on, the Global Development Initiative is showing how shared ambition can translate into practical support for development," Dima Al-Khatib, director of the United Nations Office for South-South Cooperation (UNOSSC), told Xinhua in a written interview. The initiative, she said, has "provided a platform for mobilizing partnerships, knowledge and resources in support of the 2030 Agenda for Sustainable Development." According to a United Nations Development Programme (UNDP) China publication, more than 600 projects under the Global Development Project Pool had been implemented or were in progress by the end of 2024. The associated Global Development Capital Pool had mobilized 14 billion U.S. dollars in financing commitments as of March 2025. "These mechanisms illustrate how cooperation under the GDI is supporting development financing and implementation," Al-Khatib said. An aerial drone photo taken on Sept. 29, 2025 shows the Beni Nadji raw water pre-treatment station project in the Trarza region, Mauritania. Photo: Xinhua Al-Khatib pointed to China's longstanding cooperation with UNOSSC, which spans more than two decades. "The strength of South-South cooperation lies in helping countries turn each other's experience into solutions that work for their own communities," she said. One example is the Global South-South Development Center Project, which entered its second phase in 2025 under the China-United Nations Global South-South Development Facility. Working with the China International Center for Economic and Technical Exchanges, the project aims to strengthen a network of more than 60 technical institutions to facilitate cooperation among developing countries. In West Africa, a rice initiative involving the World Food Programme, the African Union and other partners combines technology and training to improve agricultural productivity, reduce post-harvest losses and support rural livelihoods. She also highlighted cooperation on digital development, including e-commerce training that reached participants from more than 90 countries, followed by field studies in China for policymakers from 22 developing countries. With just four years left to meet the 2030 deadline, Al-Khatib said the GDI can support accelerated Sustainable Development Goal (SDG) implementation by connecting nationally identified priorities with technologies, technical expertise, financing and capacity development. A business manager of Hunan Modern Agriculture International Development Co. Ltd checks the growing condition of chili peppers with a local staff member at the Gashora Farm in Nyagatare district, Rwanda, May 22, 2025. Photo: Xinhua In September 2025, China and the United Nations announced the China-UN Global South-South Development Facility, with 10 million dollars in budget support for the 2025-2030 period. Established under the United Nations Fund for South-South Cooperation, the facility supports cooperation under the GDI in areas, including agriculture, technology and digital development, according to UNOSSC. Al-Khatib said the facility's first call for proposals, which concluded in August, attracted 107 proposals from 16 UN agencies and entities, covering 115 countries across the Global South. "The next phase may prioritize country ownership, measurable results and the adaptation and scaling of solutions suited to local circumstances," she said. Looking ahead, Al-Khatib emphasized the importance of aligning cooperation with the SDGs, UN social and environmental standards, and UN Sustainable Development Cooperation Frameworks. "The objective is to enable developing countries to adapt, co-create and sustain solutions, and share their experience across the Global South, guided by the commitment to leave no one behind," she said.

item.title: 10-minute operation highlights China's decisive crackdown on northern Myanmar telecom fraud, new documentary shows
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-05 16:31:00
The first batch of 200 Chinese telecom fraud suspects are repatriated from Myanmar to China, via Thailand, on a chartered plane on February 20, 2025. Photo: Guo Yuandan/GT After key members of the so-called "four major families" in northern Myanmar, including Wei Qingtao and Liu Zhengqi, entered Chinese territory in October 2023, a special task force moved decisively to make the arrests. The entire operation lasted just 10 minutes, according to a new documentary on China's efforts to crack down on northern Myanmar-linked telecom scams, which is set to air on Monday. Those 10 minutes marked another powerful blow in the years-long cat-and-mouse battle between Chinese police and northern Myanmar-based telecom fraud groups targeting China. They also served as a warning to telecom fraud criminals that Chinese law enforcement was coming after them, according to the documentary. The documentary, titled "The Demise of Myanmar-Based Telecom Fraud," provides a comprehensive account of how Chinese public security authorities, along with other relevant departments, launched a special campaign against crimes targeting Chinese citizens in northern Myanmar and completely dismantled criminal groups there, including the so-called "four major families." The documentary will premiere in the 6 pm slot on CCTV-1 from October 5 to 7, China Central Television (CCTV) reported. A nationwide campaign against telecom and online fraud began in early summer 2023, targeting four major scam hubs in northern Myanmar, according to the documentary. As groups in some scam hubs such as Kokang and Wa State, refused to cooperate, the command of frontline law enforcement team decided to abandon negotiations and launch direct operations. On September 26, 2023, police in Yunnan and Zhejiang arrested Bao Junfeng, a key figure linked to the scams, and members of his group in Kunming, seizing jewelry, luxury watches and high-end vehicles from his residence. Following a shooting incident involving Chinese nationals on October 20, 2023, in Kokang, China and Myanmar established a joint investigation team, with Chinese police entering scam compounds in Kokang in northern Myanmar for the first time to collect key evidence. Despite fierce fighting and Myanmar military aircraft dropping bombs nearby, Chinese police worked to prevent the evidence from being destroyed, the documentary said. The documentary also revealed that a major scam compound operated by the Ming family contained an underground shooting range where low-level scam workers were reportedly executed. Bullet-riddled walls bore evidence of killings inside the compound. Bai Yingcang, a key member of the Bai family criminal group in northern Myanmar, appears in the second episode of the documentary. Before his execution, Bai Yingcang said in an interview that these illicit industries were supporting the economy of northern Myanmar as a whole, according to the documentary. "This generation is doing it, and the next generation simply follows in the footsteps of the previous one. That's why people involved have become increasingly brazen," he said. A court in Shenzhen in South China's Guangdong Province carried out the executions in February of four leading members of a northern Myanmar-based criminal gang including Bai Yingcang, who had been sentenced to death, according to the Xinhua News Agency. Bai Yingcang said in the documentary that a "very bad atmosphere" had developed in the area at the time, where "if you weren't running scams, it meant you were doing nothing." The documentary also revealed that Chinese working groups had met three times with representatives of the so-called "four major families" in Kokang, but the meetings produced little result. "We only realized in September 2023 that China was really taking action. Chinese officials went to the border and held a meeting with us, telling us that we must eradicate telecom fraud, unconditionally," Bai Yingcang said in the documentary. Other notorious criminals appearing in the documentary include Wu Hongming, Bao Yanban, He Chuntian and She Zhijiang. And those various armed groups and major business families entrenched in northern Myanmar regarded telecom fraud as an "economic pillar" for expanding and consolidating their spheres of interest, the documentary said. With their protection, the area became home to numerous highly organized telecom fraud groups in which officials and criminals worked closely together, according to the documentary. For instance, Bao would often spread huge amounts of cash on the roof and in the yard of his home to prevent the money from becoming moldy, turning the practice into a local spectacle, according to the documentary. She Zhijiang, the alleged ringleader of the Asia Pacific New City gambling and fraud criminal group based in Myawaddy, Myanmar, also appears in the documentary. The criminal group, headed by She Zhijiang, established more than 200 online gambling platforms, attracting 330,000 Chinese nationals to participate in online gambling with more than 2.7 billion yuan ($376 million) involved, according to the documentary. The group also established multiple companies in China to recruit people for online gambling-related criminal activities and colluded with criminal groups involved in illegal payment services and underground banks both inside and outside China. She was arrested in Bangkok, Thailand, in August 2022 and successfully extradited to China in November 2025. CCTV reported that for years, multiple criminal groups led by Bai Suocheng, Wei Huairen, Liu Zhengxiang and Xu Laofa in Kokang, northern Myanmar, had established and operated numerous scam compounds targeting Chinese citizens and carried out large-scale telecom and online fraud, involving huge sums of money. The groups also developed businesses involving gambling, drugs and prostitution, organized and lured people into illegally crossing the border, and were suspected of serious violent crimes, including homicide, intentional injury and illegal detention, according to the media report. Through police and law enforcement cooperation and a series of joint operations, China and Myanmar have apprehended more than 57,000 Chinese nationals suspected of involvement in telecom fraud, dealing a devastating blow to the criminal groups operated by the so-called "four major families" in Kokang, northern Myanmar. Starting from July, 2023, Chinese authorities launched a special campaign against telecom and online fraud targeting China in northern Myanmar. On January 29, the 11 defendants in the northern Myanmar-based Ming family crime syndicate case, who were sentenced to death in September 2025, were executed. The latest statistics showed that the number of telecom fraud cases in China had fallen year on year for 11 consecutive months since October 2025. In the first half of 2026, the number of registered telecom fraud cases fell 15.6 percent year-on-year, while police conducted face-to-face anti-fraud warnings with 2.926 million people, CCTV reported. Global Times

item.title: DPP dangerously expels Chinese mainland fishing vessels; provocations must bring due consequences: Hai Feng
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-04 19:57:00
Illustration: Xia Qing/GT October 1 marked the 77th anniversary of the founding of the People's Republic of China. On this solemn day, Taiwan region's "Coast Guard Administration (CGA)" used high-pressure water cannons against a fishing boat from the Chinese mainland in waters near the Dongsha Islands, disabling the vessel's power system and leaving its crew stranded at sea for a time. No rhetorical whitewashing can hide this reckless disregard for human life Though the Democratic Progressive Party (DPP) has framed the operation as a so-called "lawful expulsion", facts can never be altered by rhetorical embellishment. Cross-Straits fishermen have long operated in relevant waters, forming established traditional fishing grounds. Against the normal temporary fishing activities of civilian vessels, the DPP dispatched large official patrol ships and continuously fired high-pressure water cannons at close range toward the vessel's wheelhouse. The reckless operations caused the boat to lose power and left crew members stranded at sea. Such excessive handling goes far beyond reasonable law-enforcement limits, and carries clear elements of danger, coercion and provocation. Maritime conditions are complex and volatile, and vessel equipment can malfunction at any time. Continuous use of high-pressure water cannons from a large patrol ship at close range against a civilian fishing vessel poses substantial risks to the hull, power systems and crew safety. Should a serious accident occur, no explanations after the fact can reverse the outcome or remedy the harm suffered by the families of those involved. Taiwan's CGA claimed it deliberately avoided crew members on the deck while spraying water, yet such arguments in no way justify its dangerous conduct. If the Taiwan side was fully aware that high-pressure water cannons carry injury risks, why did it keep firing toward the vessel's wheelhouse? Proceeding with the operation despite knowing the risks reveals cold disregard for the life and safety of fishermen from the mainland. Ordinary residents from the mainland head out to sea for fishing or recreational activities, yet the DPP treats them as targets to project a tough stance. Using civilian vessels from the mainland as props for political posturing and wagering the safety of ordinary people as bargaining chips in confrontation is outrageous. Post-rescue actions cannot offset responsibility for risks created beforehand The DPP has deliberately highlighted the so-called "humanitarian rescue" carried out by the Yunlin after the fishing boat lost power, including boarding operations and supply provision. However, this does not exempt them from liabilities over their earlier handling. It was the impact of high-pressure water cannons that disabled the vessel's power system and left mainland crew members stranded at sea in peril. Post-incident remedies cannot alter the objective fact that the danger had already materialized, nor erase the fright and hardship endured by the mainland fishermen on the water. At its core, this incident is a tangible manifestation of the DPP's long-standing confrontational agenda. In recent years, ignoring the history and reality of cross-Straits fishermen operating in these waters for generations, the DPP has repeatedly framed normal maritime activities from the mainland as alleged security threats, wrapping ordinary fishery issues in political and security narratives. As a result, the atmosphere of maritime standoffs across the Taiwan Straits keeps escalating, and the rights and interests of fishermen on both sides of the Straits have suffered severe damage. Anger must translate into well-calibrated countermeasures. It is fully understandable that netizens from the mainland are outraged by this provocative incident perpetrated by the DPP. The mainland's capacity to safeguard national sovereignty and people's rights and interests is vastly stronger than before. Faced with maritime provocations, the mainland has ample capabilities and a range of tools to defend its legitimate rights and interests, enabling reciprocal, targeted, steady and effective countermeasures. On the basis of preserving evidence, verifying facts and clarifying accountability, China will pursue legal accountability where warranted, and keep up efforts to uphold rights as appropriate. Countermeasures target the dangerous provocative acts and the responsible parties behind them, and are meant to protect the personal safety and legitimate rights and interests of people on both sides of the Taiwan Straits. The mainland does not equate the DPP's confrontational agenda with the will of Taiwan compatriots. Still less will we force ordinary people in Taiwan to bear the costs of political confrontation. Warnings must be heard, countermeasures must be forceful, and accountability must be imposed on specific responsible parties. The Chinese mainland's resolve to protect people's legitimate rights and interests, oppose dangerous provocations and crack down on "Taiwan independence" separatist acts remains unshakable. Anyone who recklessly endangers the lives and property of ordinary people must face serious consequences. Anyone bent on undermining peace and stability across the Taiwan Straits must bear full consequences for their actions. The momentum toward reunification is irresistible. Every provocation by "Taiwan independence" separatist forces will bring our countermeasures one step forward, steadily advancing the process of national reunification.

item.title: China's security ministry warns of genetic resource theft and cross-border biosecurity risks
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-04 16:37:00
Photo: Screenshot from the WeChat account of China’s Ministry of State Security China's Ministry of State Security warned on Sunday that some overseas organizations have entered ecologically sensitive areas under the guise of tourism or scientific research, or illegally collected human blood samples through purported medical testing to steal China's genetic resources and research data. In a post on its official WeChat account during the National Day holiday, the ministry highlighted cases involving blood samples, exotic pets and plant seeds, calling for greater public awareness of biosecurity risks associated with moving biological materials across borders. The ministry cited a series of major smuggling cases involving pregnant women's blood samples uncovered by Guangzhou Customs in 2025. Authorities dismantled an illicit cross-border network spanning 23 provinces, helping protect China's human genetic resources, it said. The warning also addressed the growing popularity of exotic pets and repeated attempts to bring them into China without permission. Customs authorities intercepted 5,439 batches of non-native species in passenger baggage, mail and other inbound channels in 2025, according to the ministry. In the first quarter of 2026 alone, customs authorities intercepted more than 1,000 exotic pets, including beetles, spiders, frogs, salamanders, lizards and snakes. Moving such live animals and specimens across borders requires quarantine and approval procedures, the ministry said. Plants and seeds present similar concerns. Some people buy unusual flowers or seeds overseas for personal use, while others take native seedlings and seeds abroad as gifts, overlooking the requirements governing their movement, the ministry said. In May, customs officers found 50 packets of mixed seeds in a mailed parcel declared as "personal belongings." Each packet weighed 500 grams, and the shipment contained large quantities of cannabis seeds. Customs authorities have also uncovered cases in which travelers concealed plant seedlings or disguised them as gifts to bring them into China without declaring them or submitting them for quarantine, the ministry said. Such cases carry risks beyond individual violations. Illegal imports of non-native species and unauthorized exports of native organisms or genetic resources can disrupt ecosystems, threaten agricultural production and public health and undermine biosecurity, the ministry said. It described biological genetic resources as national strategic resources and warned of the implications of their illegal export. China subjects animals, plants, related products and other regulated items moving across its borders to quarantine approval, inspection and supervision, the ministry said, warning that concealment and false declarations could seriously endanger national security. The ministry called on travelers not to carry animals, plants, seeds or other biological materials across borders without authorization. Those importing or exporting biological materials for research, teaching or other purposes should obtain the necessary permits in advance from customs and relevant agricultural or science and technology authorities, declare the materials accurately and submit them for quarantine. Members of the public should report suspected illegal cross-border movements of biological materials to the relevant authorities and assist with investigations, it added. Global Times

item.title: The more turbulent the world becomes, the more precious a peaceful China is: Global Times editorial
item.description:
Published: 2026-09-30 00:27:00
A night view of the Wangfujing pedestrian street in Beijing on September 27, 2026. Photo: VCG Peace and security are defining features of China's governance and hallmarks of Chinese modernization. Peaceful China is a light that millions upon millions of Chinese people, secure in their daily lives, shine into a world that is far from peaceful. It safeguards the everyday lives of millions of families while contributing Chinese wisdom, Chinese solutions and Chinese strength to global security governance. A working conference on the Peaceful China Initiative was held in Beijing on Monday. A recent instruction made by Chinese President Xi Jinping was conveyed at the conference. In his instruction, Xi stated that since the 18th CPC National Congress in 2012, significant progress has been made in building a safe China, making the country one of the safest in the world. Notably, peace and security are defining features of China's governance and hallmarks of Chinese modernization. Throughout human history, no country or region has achieved modernization amid persistent turmoil. From the development of a nation to the well-being of every family, peace and security are indispensable. China now ranks among the countries with the lowest rates of criminal offenses and homicide and the fewest gun-related crimes. These three distinctions provide a solid foundation for the strong sense of security enjoyed by the Chinese people. Advancing the Peaceful China Initiative in a turbulent and rapidly changing world represents a weighty commitment. The 2026 Global Peace Index shows that global peacefulness has deteriorated for 12 consecutive years, while the number of active state-based conflicts worldwide has reached its highest level since the end of World War II. According to the latest report from the United Nations High Commissioner for Refugees, as of the end of 2025, there were 117 million people forcibly displaced globally, equivalent to one in every 67 people on Earth. Meanwhile, Gallup's 2025 Global Safety Report showed that among 144 countries and regions surveyed, 94 percent of respondents in China said they feel safe walking alone at night. China has once again been recognized as one of the safest countries in the world and is the only major world power to make the list. In today's world, stability itself has become a scarce resource, and it is widely recognized as one of China's strengths. When foreign bloggers and visitors come to China, what often surprises them most is not the high-speed rail network or spectacular drone light shows, but the small details of everyday life that directly affect them: being able to go out for a late-night meal at 1 am, having a taxi driver return a phone left in the car, leaving a backpack at a café table while ordering and finding it still there upon returning, or seeing a young woman finish work, take the subway and then a bus, before walking another 10 minutes through a hutong or alley to get home. Scenes that might require suspenseful background music in an urban drama elsewhere are simply part of ordinary life in China. Data from China's National Immigration Administration showed that inbound trips made by foreign nationals exceeded 22.91 million in the first half of 2026, a surge of 20.4 percent year-on-year. There is a close connection between China's favorable public security environment and the continuing popularity of "China Travel." What particularly impresses many foreign visitors is that in China, security is not a privilege enjoyed by a small minority, but a basic public good accessible to the Chinese people. A peaceful China is no accident. It is the result of a combination of factors, including institutional strengths, governance effectiveness, cultural traditions and economic development. China's approach to security is people-centered, with development at its core. Poverty alleviation, medical insurance, social security, compulsory education and employment support all help give people confidence that their lives can continue to improve. From pushing to dismantle the "four major families" of criminal rings in northern Myanmar to better safeguarding food safety; from cracking down in accordance with the law on crimes targeting the elderly and children to continuously strengthening the public security prevention and control system; and from resolving disputes at their source to identifying and addressing public safety hazards, the advancement of the Peaceful China Initiative has continuously responded to people's evolving expectations for security. The results can be felt in people's everyday lives. Efforts to advance the Peaceful China Initiative to a higher level have extended into every urban community and every rural village, reaching the "last mile" of public security. The "Chinese sense of security" also stems from goodwill within society and a sense of civic responsibility found in the social atmosphere: Foreign tourists who lose their phones are able to get them back, and delivery workers report suspicious packages when they spot them. Recently, the positive perception that "Chinese people don't steal phones" has continued to gain traction on overseas social media, with foreign netizens recommending that wherever you travel in the world, look for a Chinese person first if you need someone to take your photo. Under the Peaceful China Initiative, China has not only become one of the world's safest major countries, but has also allowed the world to encounter more and more civic-minded Chinese people. Peaceful China is a light that millions upon millions of Chinese people, secure in their daily lives, shine into a world that is far from peaceful. It is the collective glow of more than 1.4 billion people that forms the strongest and the most dazzling foundation of a peaceful China. The more turbulent the world becomes, the more precious a peaceful China is. As a major country of more than 1.4 billion people, China unwaveringly implements a holistic approach to national security, maintains long-term social stability, and creates an environment in which people can live and work in peace and contentment - that itself is a significant contribution to global peace and security. A peaceful China is not only a shining national calling card, but also a vivid example of China promoting the building of a community with a shared future for humanity. It safeguards the everyday lives of millions of families while contributing Chinese wisdom, Chinese solutions and Chinese strength to global security governance.
